title: Yunus the Scribe and the Caliph Walid
summary: Yunus the Scribe was the most celebrated calligrapher and musician of Medina, renowned for his mastery of the reed pen and his deep knowledge of ancient melodies.
keywords: yunus the scribe and the caliph walid bin sahl
full_text:
Yunus the Scribe was the most celebrated calligrapher and musician of Medina, renowned for his mastery of the reed pen and his deep knowledge of ancient melodies.

The Umayyad Caliph Walid ibn Yazid, an ardent patron of poetry and music, heard of Yunus’s renown and dispatched a royal messenger with a thousand dinars, inviting the scribe to Damascus.

When Yunus was ushered into the royal palace, the Caliph sat upon a raised dais behind a screen of embroidered damask. The Caliph commanded: 'Let the scribe transcribe this ancient ode upon parchment in the imperial Thuluth script, and then sing the melody upon the lute.'

Yunus sat upon the marble floor, dipped his reed pen into fragrant gall-nut ink, and inscribed the verses upon gazelle-skin parchment with such breathtaking symmetry, balance, and artistic majesty that the script appeared like pearls strung upon silk.

Then, taking his lute, he sang the ancient verses with such soulful resonance, delicate modulation, and emotional depth that the Caliph drew back the screen with tears in his eyes.

'By heavens, Yunus!' exclaimed the monarch. 'Your pen writes like an angel, and your lute speaks to the soul! You have brought the fragrant breeze of the Medina palm groves into my court.'

The Caliph rewarded Yunus with ten thousand gold dinars, an estate in the fertile oasis of Ghouta, and made him the chief master of the imperial scribes, demonstrating that artistic mastery is a passport to the highest councils of civilization.
moral: Artistic excellence, refined calligraphy, and moral character win the enduring favor of monarchs.
